questions.title: How could the government appeal the district court’s pretrial dismissal of a criminal indictment?
questions.question_body: I’m confused about the procedural posture here. The district court dismissed the superseding indictment before trial, and then the United States appealed to the Fifth Circuit. In criminal cases I thought government appeals were limited because of double jeopardy concerns. What is the source of appellate jurisdiction for this kind of government appeal, and why doesn’t the Double Jeopardy Clause block it at this stage?

questions.title: Why does the Fifth Circuit review the sufficiency of an indictment de novo and assume all allegations are true?
questions.question_body: The opinion says review is de novo and that the court must take the indictment’s allegations as true to decide whether an offense has been stated. I’m having trouble understanding why the appellate court does not look at whether the government can actually prove the pump-and-dump scheme. Is this just a Rule 12 pleading question, and how is that different from reviewing evidentiary sufficiency after a conviction?

questions.title: Why is 'standing' not really discussed in a criminal fraud case like this?
questions.question_body: One thing that confuses me is that the opinion focuses on whether the indictment alleges deprivation of 'money or property,' but it never really talks about standing. If the alleged victims are the defendants’ social-media followers, do those followers need some kind of standing or legally recognized injury for the prosecution to go forward? Or is 'standing' basically the wrong concept in a criminal case, with the real question being whether the statute protects the kind of property interest the government says was targeted?

questions.title: Why does the court interpret 18 U.S.C. § 1348 by borrowing mail and wire fraud doctrine?
questions.question_body: The opinion says there is scant Fifth Circuit caselaw on the securities fraud statute, so courts rely on mail and wire fraud cases because § 1348 'borrows key concepts' from those statutes. I’m not sure how strong that move is as a matter of statutory interpretation. Is the court saying the text is materially similar enough that terms like 'scheme to defraud' and 'intent to defraud' carry over automatically, or is this more of an analogy? Why is it legitimate to import those doctrines instead of reading § 1348 more independently?

questions.title: Why did the court say this indictment alleges deprivation of money or property rather than just a loss of valuable economic information?
questions.question_body: The district court seemed to think the defendants only deprived followers of truthful trading information, which sounds like the kind of 'right to control' theory rejected in Ciminelli. But the Fifth Circuit says the indictment goes further because it alleges followers were induced to buy securities and thus parted with money. I’m struggling with the line here. If the misrepresentation affects the victim’s decision-making, why isn’t that still just a dressed-up right-to-control theory? What exactly made this a valid fraudulent-inducement theory instead?

questions.title: How does Kousisis let the court find 'intent to defraud' when the defendants allegedly meant to profit, not to cause net loss?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeats the Fifth Circuit formulation that intent to defraud means intent to deceive and intent to cause some harm from the deceit. But then it says, relying on Kousisis, that the fraud statutes do not require the defendant to seek net pecuniary loss to the victim. I’m having trouble reconciling those ideas. If the followers received securities in exchange for their money, what is the 'harm' the court thinks is enough? Did Kousisis effectively redefine the harm requirement, or is the court saying inducement to part with money under false pretenses is itself the harm?

questions.title: Why is the fraud 'complete' once the victim is induced to part with money, even if the victim receives something of equal market value?
questions.question_body: The opinion quotes Kousisis for the proposition that fraud is complete when the defendant has induced the deprivation of money or property by materially false pretenses, regardless of whether the victim suffered a net pecuniary loss. That feels counterintuitive to me in the pump-and-dump setting. If a follower buys a stock at the market price and gets the shares they paid for, why is that enough property deprivation for federal fraud? Is the idea that the law protects the victim’s control over the payment itself, so the fraudulent inducement taints the transfer even if there is nominally equivalent value on the other side?

questions.title: Does the indictment need to identify specific victims or specific trades to adequately allege securities fraud?
questions.question_body: The opinion says an indictment is sufficient if it alleges each material element, fairly informs the defendant, and protects against double jeopardy. Here the alleged scheme involved social-media followers broadly, not necessarily a small set of named victims. I’m confused about how specific the indictment has to be. Does the government need to identify which followers bought which securities based on which posts, or is it enough to allege the general pump-and-dump scheme and the defendants’ use of misleading posts to induce purchases?

questions.title: If the substantive § 1348 counts are adequately alleged, does that automatically save the § 1349 conspiracy count too?
questions.question_body: The defendants were charged both with substantive securities fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The Fifth Circuit mainly analyzes whether the indictment alleges a scheme and intent to defraud under § 1348. I’m not sure how that analysis maps onto the conspiracy charge under § 1349. Does the government also have to allege an agreement with some specificity beyond the underlying fraudulent conduct, and does § 1349 require an overt act like the general conspiracy statute does?

questions.title: Is there any due process or vagueness problem with applying § 1348 to social-media 'pump and dump' activity through mail/wire fraud concepts?
questions.question_body: A broader constitutional issue I’m wondering about is fair notice. The court reads § 1348 using mail and wire fraud precedents and then applies that framework to online stock promotion and secret selling. Could a defendant argue that this stretches the statute too far and creates a vagueness or due process problem, especially after the Supreme Court has warned against expansive fraud theories like the right-to-control theory in Ciminelli? Why does the Fifth Circuit seem comfortable that this application of the statute gives constitutionally adequate notice?

questions.title: Why did the court treat the followers’ purchase money as the relevant property interest instead of the securities market as a whole?
questions.question_body: In securities cases I usually think about harm to the integrity of the market or to counterparties generally. This opinion focuses very specifically on the defendants’ followers being induced to purchase securities. Why did the court frame the protected property interest that way? Is it because, after Ciminelli and Kousisis, the safest theory is to identify a concrete transfer of money from particular investors rather than rely on a more abstract market-manipulation theory?

questions.title: How does the Fifth and Sixth Amendment indictment standard shape what the appellate court can and cannot decide here?
questions.question_body: The opinion says an indictment must allege each material element, fairly inform the defendant of the charges, and provide protection against future prosecutions. I know this connects to constitutional indictment rights, but I’m unclear on the practical effect. When the Fifth Circuit reverses the dismissal, is it saying only that the grand jury charged a legally valid offense, not that the defendants actually committed fraud? How do the Fifth Amendment grand jury requirement and the Sixth Amendment notice function explain the court’s narrow focus on the face of the indictment?
